newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FEATURE-Politics slows return of China stowaways.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Politics slows return of China stowaways.

text.p: When Chen Hong left her home in China for Taiwan nine months ago, she dreamt of making a lot of money and returning home in time to give birth to her baby.
Those dreams shattered with her arrest by Taiwan authorities along with other mainland Chinese stowaways on a tiny fishing boat after it was spotted by coastal patrol vessels.
Instead of returning rich to her home province of Sichuan, she was 40,000 yuan (US$4,800) poorer -- the price of the boat ride -- and her baby was born in a Taiwan detention centre.
"My friend told me it was easy to make money in Taiwan," Chen told Reuters recently in the Hsinchu Mainlander's Detention Centre in northern Taiwan.
"So I asked my friend's friend to help me get on a boat," Chen said as she cradled her two-month-old baby girl.
Chen said she now regretted her decision.
"I want to be sent home as soon as possible," she said. "I will never come here again."

Chen and her baby are two of 35,085 illegal migrants from China who have been detained in Taiwan since 1987, when a thaw in political tensions between the longtime rivals triggered a wave of human traffic across the Taiwan strait.

Taiwan officials have voiced concern over the influx of illegal mainland migrants, saying Taiwan taxpayers have paid about T$110 million (US$4 million) a year in detention and repatriation costs for mainland stowaways. DETAINEES CURRENTLY AWAITING REPATRIATION FROM TAIWAN
About 500 mainlanders are awaiting repatriation in Taiwan's three detention centres.
Detention officials said progress had been slowed by the lack of a formal repatriation pact between Taipei and Beijing -- which have not been on speaking terms for two years.

Beijing froze semi-official bilateral negotiations 24 months ago to protest a landmark private visit to the United States in mid-1995 by Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui, seen by communist leaders as seeking the island's independence from China.
Taiwan, still ruled by the Chinese Nationalists, is seen by China as a renegade province since a 1949 civil war split forced the defeated Nationalists into exile on the island.

Beijing has stonewalled Taipei's calls to resume talks about repatriation of hijackers and stowaways and other technical issues, saying no dialogue is possible until Taiwan stops engaging in what China calls "splittist" activities.
Analysts have said Beijing was unlikely to resume talks with Taiwan soon because of its single-minded focus on Hong Kong's July 1 return to China after 156 years as a British colony.
In addition to the mainland stowaways, uncertainty clouds the fate of 16 mainland people who hijacked commercial airplanes to Taiwan in the early 1990s.

One of them, Han Fengying, who served four years in prison for hijacking a Chinese airliner to Taiwan with her husband, remains in custody at the Hsinchu detention centre despite her parole because she is has no legal residency rights.

"I didn't give much thought (about my future). I didn't choose to come here in the first place," said the 33-year-old Han, explaining that it was her husband's idea to come to Taiwan and she simply wanted the family to be together.
That dream exploded. Husband Yang Mingde remains in prison and their son Yang Yang, just six when they commandeered the plane on September 30, 1993, lives in a state-funded orphanage.
"I only want to have a little more freedom, to be able to take care of my child," Han said at the Hsinchu centre.
Han's stay in Taiwan may be nearing an end, but her problems could get much worse.
Taipei said on (June 17 that she and another paroled air pirate, Huang Shugang, soon would be sent home, reciprocating for Beijing's May repatriation of a Taiwan hijacker.
Han and Huang could both face new trials at home on air piracy charges -- a capital offence in communist China.

Beijing in May returned Taiwan air pirate Liu Shan-chung -- completing the first cross-strait hijacker repatriation despite its own two-year-old freeze on talks with Taiwan and the absence of formal repatriation pact.
Chang King-yuh, Taiwan's top maker of policy toward China, said his cabinet-level Mainland Affairs Council had agreed to consider repatriating Han and Huang on a case-by-case basis.
Chang also urged China to reopen talks and set up a formal repatriation channel to handle future cases.
"If mainland China cannot get her own house in order, it will cause great trouble in neighbouring countries," Chang said. "We believe the problem should be solved by whoever caused the problem."
